commentary: Having finished treating being as it is divided among the ten categories, Aristotle turns to a further division of being that cuts across all of them: being as potency and being as actuality. Aquinas opens by sorting out the many things people mean by 'can' or 'power.' Some are called potencies only by a loose analogy, as when geometers speak of one magnitude being the 'power' of another; these he sets aside as not truly relevant. What remains are potencies properly so called, and all of these, he insists, trace back to one primary sense: an active potency, which is a source or principle of change in something else, or in the same thing insofar as it is other than itself. From this primary notion of active power, Aquinas shows how the correlative notion of passive potency follows — the capacity in a thing to be acted upon and altered by an outside source. He is careful to note that a thing does not, properly speaking, act upon itself as one and the same subject, since acting and being acted upon require some real distinction between mover and moved. Finally Aquinas explains impotency, or incapacity, as simply the privation corresponding to potency: wherever a power could belong to a subject by nature, its absence counts as a privation only if the subject is of a kind that should have had it. This opening lectio thus lays the groundwork for the entire book by establishing act and potency as principles that run through every category of being, prior even to the distinction of substance from accident.

Aquinas next distinguishes potencies according to the kind of subject in which they reside: some belong to things without soul, some to living things, and among these, some are guided by reason and some are not. This division lets Aristotle explain a striking asymmetry. A non-rational power, like the capacity of fire to heat, produces only a single, fixed effect — fire cannot also cool. But a rational power, such as the medical art, is capable of opposite effects: the same science that can restore health can also, if misapplied, induce disease. Aquinas explains why: a rational account, or 'formula,' in the mind grasps a thing and its privation by the very same act of understanding, though not in the same way — the science is directed essentially toward the positive term (health) and only accidentally, by way of contrariety, toward its absence (sickness). Because the soul possessing this rational principle can originate motion toward either of two contrary termini from one and the same source of knowledge, the rational art is naturally suited to opposite effects, unlike a merely natural power tied to one determinate outcome. Aquinas underscores that this is not a defect in reason but rather evidence of reason's higher, more universal mode of operating, since it possesses the formula of both a thing and its lack. He closes by noting that the power to do a thing well presupposes the power merely to do it, though not conversely — one can do a thing without doing it well, but not do it well without being able to do it at all.

Here Aquinas takes up Aristotle's confrontation with the Megarian school, who held that a thing has a power only while it is actually exercising it — so that a builder who is not currently building would not really be capable of building at all. Aquinas lays out the absurdities this view generates. First, no one could be called an artisan except while working, so that a builder loses and instantly reacquires his skill every time he stops and starts. Second, sensible qualities like heat or sweetness would exist only while actually being perceived, collapsing into the relativism associated with Protagoras. Third, a sighted person not currently seeing would have to be called blind, and blind again and again throughout the day. Fourth, and most seriously, the Megarian position destroys the very possibility of motion and coming-to-be, since whatever is not presently in a given state could never truly be said capable of reaching it. Having demolished this position, Aquinas explains Aristotle's constructive alternative: potency and actuality are genuinely distinct, and a thing can rightly be called potential — capable of being or of some activity — provided that positing it as actually so involves no impossibility. This criterion, that nothing impossible follows from supposing the potency actualized, becomes the working definition of potency henceforth in the book, and Aquinas stresses that it is compatible with a thing's capacity never in fact being realized, since potency does not entail future actuality, only the absence of intrinsic contradiction.

Aquinas continues unpacking the criterion just established by clarifying an important distinction between what is merely false and what is strictly impossible. Something can be false yet still possible — it is false that a certain man is standing, but nothing prevents his standing. By contrast, some suppositions are not merely false but impossible outright, because affirming them as actual entails a contradiction; Aquinas takes Aristotle's example of the diagonal of a square being commensurable with its side, which cannot even be supposed actual without absurdity, unlike the mere falsehood that it is being measured right now. Aquinas then walks through the more technical, syllogism-like argument Aristotle constructs about possibility: if the being of A necessarily entails the being of B, then the mere possibility of A must likewise entail the possibility of B, since if B could not possibly be, positing A as actual would generate an impossibility, which would show A itself was never truly possible. Aquinas treats this as establishing a general logical law governing how possibility distributes across valid entailments, reinforcing that potency is not an arbitrary or loose way of speaking but tracks strict relations of non-contradiction. This careful logical excursus, in Aquinas's reading, is not a digression but Aristotle's way of making the earlier definition of potency rigorous, so that the whole subsequent treatment of act and potency rests on a criterion that can withstand dialectical challenge.

Aquinas notes Aristotle's threefold division of the origins of potencies: some are simply innate, like the senses; some come through practice or repeated exercise, like the flute-player's skill; and some are acquired by instruction, like the arts. Potencies of the second and third sort require the agent first to perform the relevant acts before the stable power is possessed, whereas natural, passive potencies like sensation need no such prior exercise. Aquinas then addresses a question central to the book: given that a rational potency is indifferently open to contrary effects, what determines which effect actually follows when the potency is exercised? Since a rational power such as an art or science could equally produce either of two opposite results, something beyond the bare power itself must settle the matter, or else contrary effects would follow simultaneously, which is impossible. Aquinas explains that this further determining factor is appetite or will: whichever of the two outcomes the agent decisively desires, under the right conditions — namely, when the patient is suitably disposed and no external hindrance intervenes — is what actually comes to be. Non-rational potencies, lacking any such internal principle of determination, act of necessity whenever agent and patient are duly conjoined, and so are restricted to one effect only. This lectio thus supplies part of the deep structure behind Aquinas's later, fuller treatment of free will and voluntary action: rational agency requires an additional principle of self-determination that mere natural causality does not.

Turning at last from potency to actuality itself, Aquinas observes that Aristotle refuses to give actuality a strict definition, since it is among the most basic notions and definitions must proceed from what is prior and better known. Instead Aristotle proceeds by induction and proportional example, and Aquinas walks through each: as the statue of Hermes is to the block of wood from which it might be carved, as the half-line is to the undivided whole line, as one who is awake is to one asleep, as one who is actually seeing is to one who merely has the power of sight — in each pair, the second term is potential and the first actual. Aquinas notes Aristotle's caution that actuality is said only by analogy across such varied cases, not univocally, since some pairs relate as form to matter and others as an operation to its capacity. He then addresses two special cases, the infinite and the void, whose potential existence differs from ordinary cases: the infinite never comes to be actual as a completed whole but exists potentially only in the sense that its process of division can always continue, its potency serving thought rather than terminating in an actual separate existence. Finally, and most importantly for the book's larger argument, Aquinas explains Aristotle's distinction between incomplete motions (kinesis) — such as walking, building, or being healed, none of which possess their end within themselves at any given instant — and complete actualities (energeia), such as seeing, understanding, or living well, in which the activity and its perfection coincide at every moment it occurs. This distinction between imperfect process and perfect act becomes central to Aquinas's later account of contemplative happiness.

Aquinas here takes up the question of precisely when something should be called potentially another thing, since not every subject is potentially just anything whatsoever. Earth is not yet potentially a man, nor even potentially a statue, until it has undergone the intervening transmutations needed to prepare it. Aquinas distinguishes proximate from remote potency: a thing is potentially something in the full sense only when nothing further needs to be added, removed, or changed for it to become that thing through its own agency or through an external agent already at hand, without which nothing impossible would follow. Seed, for instance, is not yet potentially a man in this proximate sense, since it must first be deposited and undergo considerable change; only once it has developed appropriately does it become proximately potential. Aquinas then draws out Aristotle's linguistic observation about denominative or 'adjectival' predication: we do not call a casket 'earth' but rather call the wood it is made from 'wooden,' and its ultimate matter is named by an adjectival, indeterminate form of speech rather than a straightforward substantial name — signifying that this underlying matter stands to the finished thing precisely as potency to act. Pursuing this chain of matter behind matter, Aquinas explains, brings us finally to prime matter, which is no longer denominated from anything further behind it, since it is the ultimate subject, in itself utterly indeterminate, bearing no formal determination of its own apart from the forms and accidents received into it.

This long chapter draws the book's central conclusion, and Aquinas devotes several lectiones to unpacking its threefold demonstration that actuality is unqualifiedly prior to potency. First, actuality is prior in intelligibility or definition, since potency can only be defined by reference to the corresponding act — to be capable of building is defined as being able to produce the act of building, so the concept of the act must already be grasped first. Second, actuality is prior in time, in a qualified sense: though this individual potential man precedes his own actuality, some other thing already actual (a father, a prior craftsman) must always precede and produce whatever exists potentially, since nothing brings itself from potency into act without some pre-existing actual cause; Aquinas notes here Aristotle's resolution of the sophistic puzzle about how a learner can begin practicing an art he does not yet possess, explaining that in any process of becoming, some portion of the end is already partially actual. Third, and most fundamentally, actuality is prior in perfection and substantial being, since whatever comes later in a process of generation is more complete in form, and potency exists entirely for the sake of the act toward which it tends, as sight exists for the sake of seeing rather than seeing for the sake of possessing sight. Within this, Aquinas develops the distinction between operations that terminate within the agent itself, such as seeing, understanding, and willing — the very operations in which Aquinas locates beatitude — and those that pass into external matter, like building. Finally, Aquinas follows Aristotle in showing that eternal, incorruptible things are pure actuality without any admixture of potency, since every potency is inherently a potency for opposites, including non-being, so that anything genuinely eternal can involve no real potency to not-exist; from this he also derives Aristotle's rejection of separately subsisting Platonic Forms, which would absurdly have to be inferior in actuality to the very sciences and motions that merely participate them.

Aquinas explains Aristotle's argument that actuality surpasses potency not only in being but in value. A mere capacity is, by its nature, indifferently open to opposite outcomes — the same power that can produce health can equally produce sickness, the same capacity that can build can also destroy. But contrary actualities can never coexist in the same subject at once, and since among any pair of contraries the good one must be superior, while bare potency as such is neutral between them, the actuality that determinately realizes the good must be better than the undetermined capacity for it. Aquinas notes the parallel but reversed case for evil: since evil, too, only befalls a subject already having potency toward it, actual evil is worse than potential evil, yet evil itself has no independent nature or substance of its own — it is always something posterior, a privation attaching to potency, and for this reason no eternal, purely actual being can admit any evil, defect, or corruption whatsoever. Aquinas then turns to Aristotle's illustration from geometry: theorems that could in principle be discovered simply by dividing a given figure are not thereby already known, but come to be known only once the geometer actually performs the construction — drawing the auxiliary line, for instance, that makes a theorem about the triangle's angles evident at a glance. Aquinas reads this as confirming that potency is brought to light and actualized only through some actually existing operation, here the geometer's own actual reasoning, reinforcing throughout the chapter that actuality, not potency, is the more excellent and more truly explanatory principle.

In the closing lectio, Aquinas explains a further sense of being and non-being beyond the categories and beyond act and potency: being and non-being as true and false. Truth and falsity, he explains, follow upon the intellect's act of combining or dividing concepts in judgment, and are measured by whether that combination or division corresponds to how things actually stand in reality — thinking separate what is really separate, or united what is really united, yields truth, and thinking the reverse yields error; crucially, it is the state of the thing that makes the judgment true, not the judgment that makes the thing so. Regarding necessary or eternal states of affairs, Aquinas notes that the corresponding judgment, once true, cannot become false, nor once false become true, whereas concerning contingent matters the same statement may be true at one time and false at another. He then turns to Aristotle's more difficult case of simple, non-composite realities — essences grasped by a single act of understanding rather than by combining subject and predicate. Here, Aquinas explains, falsity in the strict sense cannot occur, since there is no composition to misjudge; the intellect either attains such an essence, which counts as truth or 'contact,' or else fails to attain it at all, which is simply ignorance rather than positive error, unlike the more complete privation involved in blindness. Aquinas concludes that such simple, wholly actual substances, being incapable of any composition of potency with act in their being, cannot come to be or cease to be, and consequently the intellect's relation to them admits no fluctuation between truth and falsity across time, only knowledge or its absence.
